What if one of the defining energy challenges of this decade isn’t heating, but cooling?

In 2021, more than half a million people died from heat exposure, an increase of more than 60% since the 1990s. Every warming scenario tells us this is only the beginning.

Cooling is often seen as a household need, but it is essential across the entire development value chain. It keeps hospitals functioning, food systems running, and businesses productive. As temperatures rise and AI, digital infrastructure, and data centres drive growing electricity demand, cooling is becoming one of the defining pressures on energy systems. I have increasingly come to see cooling not as a matter of comfort, but as critical infrastructure for human development.

In this video, I share three reflections:

🔥 Heat is a justice issue. More than 1 billion people are already at high risk because they lack access to adequate cooling, with the greatest needs concentrated across the Global South, regions that have contributed the least to historical emissions. As temperatures rise, heat is amplifying existing inequalities and increasing risks for the most vulnerable communities.

📊 Cooling is a development multiplier. Cooling protects vaccines and medicines, keeps hospitals functioning, reduces food loss, and enables children to learn in safe classrooms. Today, around 13% of food is lost between harvest and retail, much of it because of inadequate cold chains.

⚡ The future of cooling depends on sustainable energy. Without action, global cooling demand could more than triple by 2050. Yet a sustainable cooling practices could cut cooling-related emissions by 64% while expanding access.

There is reason for optimism. Between 2015 and 2022, the number of countries with national cooling policies increased from 21 to 176. But policies alone are not the finish line. The next challenge is implementation at the speed and scale that today’s climate reality demands.

In a warming world, achieving SDG 7 is no longer only about expanding access to energy. It is about ensuring that energy protects lives, strengthens resilience, and enables development for everyone.

#EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7 #Cooling #JustEnergyTransition

The promise of green growth lies in turning the next wave of development investment into productive capacity, jobs and higher-value industries in developing countries. That opportunity is within reach, but the task is urgent: over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age, while current trajectories are expected to create only 400 million jobs and the sustainable development financing gap remains around $4 trillion a year.

Agro-value chains show what this can look like in practice. They connect production to higher-value activity after the farmgate, where reliable and affordable clean energy can reduce losses, strengthen SMEs, support local industry and help producer communities retain more value. Agrifood systems use about 30% of globally available energy, with around 70% of that energy used after the farmgate, making clean energy central to inclusive growth.

This week, I look forward to joining the HLPF 2026 side event “Powering Green Growth: Inclusive Solutions for Energy and Industry through Agro-Value Chains,” where we will explore how clean energy, sustainable industrialization and stronger partnerships can advance inclusive economic growth and progress on SDGs 7, 9 and 17.

What does it mean for the energy transition to reach the grid, the data centre and the electric vehicle, but still not reach the kitchen?
 
Today’s discussion brought that challenge into focus at the 2026 HLPF Regional Satellite Event, “From Commitment to Implementation: A Regional Dialogue on Coordinated UN-Energy Action for Clean Cooking.”
 
Clean cooking remains one of the most urgent and overlooked development challenges. While the world is investing over US$2.2 trillion in the energy transition, 2 billion people still cook with polluting fuels, and 1.8 billion are projected to remain without clean cooking in 2030.
 
The discussions made clear that clean cooking sits at the heart of health, gender equality, climate action and human dignity. Household air pollution caused 2.9 million deaths in 2021, including 309,000 children under five, while women and girls continue to carry the burden of smoke exposure and fuel collection.
 
Yet progress is possible: since 2010, India, China and Indonesia have driven 80% of the global reduction in the clean cooking access gap.
 
The conversation also reinforced the need for smarter, more targeted delivery. Of the 2 billion people without clean cooking access, 1.5 billion live in rural areas, and the top 20 access-deficit countries account for around three-quarters of the global gap. Using geospatial analytics and AI-driven tools such as the Clean Energy Equity Index, UNDP helps countries identify underserved communities and target clean energy investments where they are needed most.
 
But delivery also needs finance and systems that can turn commitments into results. Universal clean cooking access requires around US$8 billion annually, while the cost of inaction is estimated at US$2.4 trillion each year. Examples from Ghana, Rwanda and Morocco show how clear targets, public finance and delivery systems can move clean cooking from pledge to practice.
 
I left the discussion with one clear reflection: the energy transition cannot be judged only by how much power we generate, but by whether it reaches the kitchens, classrooms, clinics and communities still being left behind.
 
#HLPF2026 #SDG7 #CleanCooking #CleanEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #UNEnergy #UNDP

The world is proving that clean energy can scale at record speed. For me, the real test now is whether it can reach the countries and communities still being left behind.
 
I was pleased to participate today in the HLPF 2026 Special Event: “Implementing the Global Plan of Action for the Decade of Sustainable Energy for All to 2030,” which also marked the launch of the UN-Energy Work Programme 2026–2030.
 
The launch comes at a decisive moment for SDG 7. Clean energy is scaling faster than ever: in 2025, the world added 692 GW of new renewable electricity capacity, the largest annual increase on record, with renewables accounting for almost 97% of all new power capacity installed globally.
 
Yet progress remains too uneven. Around 655 million people still lack electricity, nearly 2 billion still rely on polluting cooking fuels, and installed renewable capacity stands at 544 watts per person globally, compared with just 33.6 watts in low-income countries.
 
This is the challenge of the final stretch to 2030.
 
The Global Plan of Action provides the roadmap. The UN-Energy Work Programme provides the coordination platform to help turn that roadmap into delivery through foresight, acceleration, partnerships, data, convening and communications.
 
What stood out to me is how deeply connected these issues have become: energy access, clean cooking, AI and digitalisation, critical minerals, green jobs, finance, gender equality and industrial development. Fragmented action will not deliver the speed or scale required.
 
SDG 7 must also move beyond access to become an engine of opportunity. The global energy sector now employs 76 million people, including at least 16.6 million in renewable energy, but many of these opportunities remain concentrated in economies with established clean-energy value chains.
 
Finance must also reach those furthest behind. International public finance for clean energy in developing countries reached US$24.6 billion in 2024, yet LDCs, LLDCs and SIDS received less than 30% of these flows.
 
At UNDP, we see this through our work supporting 398 energy projects in 131 countries: helping countries turn policy into investment, and investment into development outcomes.
 
The years to 2030 must be about delivery with speed, scale and equity.
 
#SDG7 #HLPF2026 #JustEnergyTransition #RenewableEnergy #UNEnergy #UNDP

Every year, inadequate cold chains waste 526 million tonnes of food, enough to feed 950 million people. Farmers lose around 15% of their income because they cannot access higher-value markets.
 
How much value are we leaving on the table?
 
The answer depends on one critical factor: energy.
 
It was a pleasure to join the Permanent Mission of Malaysia and CPOPC at the HLPF 2026 side event on Powering Green Growth: Inclusive Solutions for Energy and Industry through Agro-Value Chains.
 
Nearly 30% of global energy is used by agri-food systems, and more than 70% of that energy is consumed after food leaves the farm in cooling, processing, transport, and logistics. This is where countries capture value, build competitive industries, and create better jobs.
 
The real opportunity is not producing more. It is producing more value. Clean energy enables higher-value processing, stronger cold chains, digital and AI-enabled services, and the next generation of green jobs. Already 375 million people work in off-farm agri-food activities, and as agricultural production grows by 14% over the next decade, geospatial intelligence can help direct investment where renewable energy creates the greatest economic impact.
 
At UNDP, we are helping make that happen. In Nepal, our first agrovoltaic farming system supports more than 450 households with renewable energy, irrigation, and higher-value agriculture. In Kenya, our partnership with UNCDF is expected to mobilize US$31 million for solar cold storage, strengthening local value chains and reducing post-harvest losses.
 
Green growth is ultimately about turning clean energy into productive capital, connecting renewable energy with agriculture, finance and local enterprise so countries create more value at home rather than exporting it abroad.
 
Thank you to the Permanent Missions of Malaysia and Indonesia, CPOPC and fellow panelists for an excellent discussion.
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #SDG7 #SDG9

As clean energy technologies advance at record speed, can our institutions, financing models and energy systems keep pace?

Over the next five years, global electricity demand is expected to grow around 50% faster than it did over the previous decade, driven by electrification, industry, AI and digitalization. Yet financing costs for renewable energy projects remain two to three times higher in many developing economies than in advanced economies. The opportunity to accelerate development through clean energy has never been greater. Delivering on that promise requires faster implementation, stronger institutions and financing that reaches the countries where demand is growing fastest.

US$2 trillion was invested in clean energy globally last year, yet international public clean energy finance for developing countries amounted to just US$24.6 billion.
 
At today's Building Investment Plans to Unlock Climate Finance for Vulnerable Nations dialogue at #HLPF2026, I posed a simple question: Are SIDS and LDCs truly lacking bankable projects, or are we failing to recognize where value is being created?
 
The economics of the energy transition are increasingly compelling. Renewable electricity costs are projected to fall 30% by 2030, while electricity demand over the next five years is expected to grow 50% faster than over the previous decade. Capital is available. Demand is growing.
 
The opportunity is to connect the two.
 
That starts with better data. UNDP's satellite analysis identified 1.18 billion people living in energy poverty, around 60% more than those captured by conventional electricity access metrics. Better intelligence helps reveal hidden demand, reduce investment risk, and direct finance where it can deliver the greatest development impact.
 
It also means financing economic value creation. Clean energy should power industries, transport, agriculture, and digital economies that create jobs and strengthen resilience. This matters because manufacturing value added per capita in LDCs has increased by more than 40% since 2015, yet it remains far below the global average.
 
It also requires the right conditions for private investment. With around 80% of public clean energy finance coming as debt and only 5% supporting risk mitigation, countries need policy reform, blended finance, and tools like UNDP’s Energy Finance Innovation Labs to build investable pipelines and reduce risk.
 
Investment plans become bankable pipelines when we stop financing energy as a standalone asset and start financing the economic value it unlocks.
 
That is UNDP 's role: helping countries build the institutions, markets, and investment ecosystems that turn clean energy into jobs, industries, resilience, and long-term development.
 
My thanks to SEforALL and the Governments of Australia, Barbados, Fiji, and Tuvalu for convening this timely dialogue ahead of Pre-COP31 and for advancing the broader conversation on unlocking climate finance for vulnerable countries in the lead-up to COP31.
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #PreCOP31 #RisingUpForSIDS

Ten years ago, one in every 100 cars sold worldwide was electric. Last year, it was one in four. That is one of the fastest technology transitions in the history of energy.

But what is the real meaning of mobility?

It is more than moving people—it is about connecting them to opportunity. Today, less than half of the world's population has access to public transport, and in many developing cities fewer than half of jobs can be reached within one hour. Mobility expands access to jobs, education and healthcare, strengthening social cohesion by connecting communities and national cohesion by linking regions, reducing inequalities and expanding economic opportunity.

E-mobility is therefore about more than replacing fuel cars with electric ones. If we're redesigning how we move, why not redesign the spaces we move through? In many cities, roads and parking already occupy up to 30–40% of urban land—space that could instead support people, nature and more resilient communities.

Imagine cities with fewer parking lots, wider sidewalks, more bus lanes, green corridors, urban forests and vibrant public spaces. The energy transition is also an opportunity to rethink the built environment itself. Electrification should be the starting point for cities built around people—not simply an electric version of today's car-centric model. In the Global South, where most future urban growth will occur, this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to build cities differently.

Yesterday, at the HLPF side event on Advancing the United Nations Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026–2035), I had the opportunity to discuss these ideas organized by Global Sustainable Transport Innovation and Knowledge Center and UNDESA.

The momentum is encouraging: EV sales in emerging economies outside China grew by around 80% in 2025, while the global EV fleet is now displacing around 1.7 million barrels of oil demand every day.

In Sri Lanka, UNDP is supporting the transition of 500,000 tuk-tuks to electric vehicles over five years—reducing fuel imports while creating new opportunities for drivers, women and vulnerable groups.

These models work because they fit local economies. They are becoming even more viable because battery pack costs have fallen by 93% since 2010.

It means recognizing that, in many countries, two- and three-wheelers may deliver the greatest development impact. It means using data and digitalization to enable smart charging and vehicle-to-grid integration, embedding e-mobility within national energy planning, accelerating public transport electrification, and creating more value in the countries where the critical minerals powering this transition are sourced.

If the future is electric, shouldn't we also redesign the spaces we move through? #UNDP #HLPF2026 #EMobility #SustainableTransport #EnergyTransition Riad Meddeb , Xie Hui , Elif Su Duygun , Tamara Rasamny تمارا الرسامني, Clement Amponsah , Hitomi Yamaguchi

72% of electricity meters in Great Britain are smart meters.

In Germany, it's just 5.5%.

That gap isn't really about technology. It's about public policy — and it says a lot about how ready each country is for what comes next.

Britain treated smart meters as essential infrastructure:
→ National deployment targets
→ Regulatory obligations on utilities
→ Investment in a shared digital communications network

Germany treated them as a consumer product:
→ Narrower deployment requirements
→ Heavier emphasis on privacy and cybersecurity
→ Costs left largely to households

The result isn't just a slower rollout in Germany. It's a different capacity to support the next phase of electrification.

Here's why that matters:

Smart meters are the gateway to the new electricity economy. Without one, you can't access variable tariffs that reward you for using power when renewables are abundant. You can't optimise solar, batteries or heat pumps. You can't take part in flexibility markets or bidirectional EV charging.

The lesson goes well beyond meters.

Countries that treat digitally enabled electricity systems as strategic national infrastructure — not optional consumer upgrades — will move faster on clean energy, energy security, and competitiveness.

Just as past generations invested collectively in roads, railways and broadband, this generation needs to invest in intelligent electricity networks.

The hardest part of this isn't technological. It's financial.

If households are left to fund this transformation mainly through higher bills, the transition will be slower, less fair, and politically harder to sustain.

Governments, regulators, utilities and capital markets should instead treat this as productive public investment — shifting the upfront cost away from households and toward long-term infrastructure financing.

Electrification is about far more than replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy.

It's about building the infrastructure for a digitally enabled, clean energy system — bringing together the two most powerful drivers of innovation and competitiveness in the twenty-first century: the green transition and the digital revolution. #Electrification #EnergyTransition #EnergySecurity #CleanEnergy #DigitalInfrastructure #Energiewende #Verkehrswende

The question I kept coming back to while moderating the discussion at the #HLPF2026 High-level Thematic Event on Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition for Equity and Resilience was a simple one:
 
Can our institutions evolve as quickly as our technologies?
 
The numbers tell an interesting story. 92% of the world's population now has access to electricity, yet the pace of electrification has slowed: Reaching universal access by 2030 will require progress at more than three times today's rate.
 
Meanwhile, the transition itself is accelerating. Renewables now generate over 30% of global electricity, solar and wind consumption has increased fivefold in the past decade, and AI could save the power sector up to USD 110 billion every year through smarter planning and operations.
 
If we have technology, innovation, what is the real bottleneck? Are we still treating electricity as the end goal, when it should be the beginning of economic transformation? 
 
I was pleased to moderate the panel discussion at today's #HLPF2026 High-level Thematic Event on Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition for Equity and Resilience, bringing together experts from the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the World Resources Institute (WRI).
 
The discussion reinforced that stronger institutions, better planning, bankable investment pipelines and financing models that reduce risk are what will determine whether innovation reaches the countries and communities that need it most. Unlocking nearly USD 1 trillion in annual private investment in emerging and developing economies will require around USD 80–100 billion of concessional finance each year.
 
My thanks to GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  and all the partners for convening this timely dialogue, to our excellent panelists, and to everyone who contributed to such a thoughtful exchange.
 
What innovation - technological, financial or institutional - will have the greatest impact on accelerating SDG 7?
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #SDG7

The discussion reinforced that stronger institutions, better planning, bankable investment pipelines and financing models that reduce risk are what will determine whether innovation reaches the countries and communities that need it most. Unlocking nearly USD 1 trillion in annual private investment in emerging and developing economies will require around USD 80–100 billion of concessional finance each year.

The next big opportunity for sustainable cities may not be only how much clean power we generate, but how well we move it, manage it and deliver it.

The scale of opportunity is enormous. Global energy investment is set to reach US$3.3 trillion in 2025, with US$2.2 trillion flowing to clean energy technologies, including renewables, grids, storage and electrification. But that investment only delivers its full value if clean power reaches people, businesses and growing cities.

Cities are already home to 3.69 billion people, around 45% of the world's population, and account for 75% of global energy use and 70% of CO₂ emissions. As cities grow, demand from cooling, buildings, electric mobility, digital services and public infrastructure will make grids central to sustainable urban planning.

This is where grids become development infrastructure.

Modern, flexible and digital grids can connect more renewable energy, reduce outages, support electric mobility, power efficient buildings, enable cooling, strengthen water and sanitation systems, improve services in underserved communities, reduce reliance on diesel backup and unlock cleaner, more productive urban economies.

Around 3,000 GW of renewable energy projects were stuck in grid connection queues in 2023. Unlocking that power through better planning, digital systems, storage and grid investment could turn stranded clean energy into jobs, services and resilience.

By 2040, around 80 million kilometres of grids may need to be added or replaced, roughly equivalent to the entire existing global grid. This is one of the largest infrastructure opportunities of the energy transition.

For rapidly growing cities in Africa and Asia, grid investment can help avoid high-carbon lock-in and support a different urban future: cleaner air, reliable services, productive enterprises, safer streets, better cooling and more resilient communities.

As HLPF continues, the message is clear: SDG 7 and SDG 11 must be planned through the grid. Modern grids can turn clean energy ambition into sustainable urban transformation.

"The clean energy transition is unstoppable. The question is whether the development transition will keep pace."
 
That was the defining message emerging from the UN High-Level Meeting on Critical Energy Transition Minerals and the thematic roundtables at #HLPF2026.
 
Demand for critical energy transition minerals is expected to almost triple by 2030, while around US$500 billion in new mining investment will be needed by 2040. Yet between 2020 and 2024, nearly 90 percent of new refining capacity for key critical minerals was added by a single leading producer for each mineral. The challenge is no longer only securing supply. It is creating more diversified, resilient and equitable value chains that also deliver development.
 
Throughout yesterday’s  discussions, one message resonated across governments, industry, international organizations, Indigenous Peoples and civil society:
The energy transition cannot repeat yesterday's extractive model.
 
Resource-rich countries should not remain exporters of raw materials while higher-value industries, technology and jobs are created elsewhere. Critical minerals must become a catalyst for industrialization, economic diversification, decent work and long-term prosperity.
 
The conversation has moved beyond principles. It is now about implementation. 
 
The Secretary-General's Guiding Principles provide the roadmap. The task now is to translate them into country-level action through stronger institutions, financing, technology transfer, local value creation and trusted international partnerships.
 
As co-chair of the UN Joint Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, together with UNCTAD and UNEP, and with UNDP leading the Country Support Mechanism, we are working with countries to turn these principles into practical support that strengthens governance, mobilizes investment and helps countries move up mineral value chains.
 
Critical minerals can power the energy transition if we ensure they also power development.

What if Africa’s energy challenge is not only about who gets connected, but what those connections make possible?

That was the reflection I took from yesterday’s discussion on “From Evidence to Action: Accelerating Energy Access and Just Transitions in Africa,” hosted at the Permanent Representation of Nigeria.

Electricity access in sub-Saharan Africa rose from 51% in 2017 to 61% in 2023, with more than 120 million people gaining access in six years. Yet the scale of the challenge remains stark: the region still accounts for 86% of the global electricity access deficit, with 563 million people without power, while around 970 million people lack clean cooking.

The message from today was clear: energy access must become a platform for jobs, resilience, industry and a just transition.

Africa has the resources to lead this shift. The continent holds around 60% of the world’s best solar resources and more than 30% of known critical mineral reserves, yet imports over 80% of the technologies needed for renewable energy deployment. The opportunity is to turn this potential into cheaper power, local value chains, clean industries and decent jobs.

Decentralized energy systems are central to this agenda, especially in hard-to-reach communities.

Through initiatives Africa Minigrids Programme, Energy for Grwoth and Solar for Healts, and collaborating with Mission 300 partners, UNDP is helping African countries move beyond isolated pilot projects by creating the enabling environment for renewable energy system to scale through commercial investment, rural electrification and productive energy use.

Delivery must also become smarter. AI-enabled grid management can improve renewable integration by 20–30%, while geospatial planning, as seen in Rwanda, Zambia and Nigeria, can target grid, mini-grid and off-grid solutions where they best support rural electrification, agriculture, healthcare and local enterprise.

Africa’s energy future is not defined by a lack of potential, but by how quickly we can turn evidence into investment, and investment into delivery that creates jobs, strengthens local enterprise and expands shared prosperity.

Can AI become a catalyst for sustainable development without becoming a growing burden on the planet?

That was the central question from today’s 2026 HLPF side event on Advancing Digital Environmental Sustainability for SDG Implementation. As the HLPF draws to a close, the discussion reinforced that digital transformation must be integrated into the sustainable development agenda.

AI is reshaping development, but behind every algorithm lies a physical system powered by electricity, water, minerals and infrastructure. By 2030, data centres could use 945 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent of the current electricity consumption of Africa.

By 2030, AI is expected to add US$15.7 trillion to the global economy, while developing countries may capture only 10% of that value.

I shared insights from UNDP ’s report, The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries, which shows that AI’s next frontier will depend as much on energy systems as computing power. It calls for Green AI that advances people, protects the planet and expands prosperity by aligning digital investment with clean energy and national priorities.

I shared three key priorities: directing AI towards practical development challenges, building skills and innovation ecosystems that create domestic value, and embedding sustainability and accountability into investment from the outset.

Examples are emerging. In Kenya, AI-enabled energy systems are improving affordability and resilience. In Moldova, UNDP is supporting 500,000 smart meters by 2030. UNDP tools, such as the Clean Energy Equity Index and the Electricity Access Forecasting Model, are helping countries improve AI and digital planning and resilience.

My takeaway is that the Global Digital Compact must move from ambition to implementation. Beyond 2030, digital progress should be defined not by technological scale alone, but by its contribution to inclusion, resilience and sustainable development.

The race for critical energy transition minerals will shape not only the future of clean energy—it will shape the future of development, industrialization and geopolitics.

The question is whether resource-rich developing countries will simply supply the raw materials for the energy transition—or become full participants in the industries and prosperity that it creates.

That was the focus of this week’s first United Nations  High-Level Meeting on Critical Energy Transition Minerals and the subsequent meeting of the UN Task Force, marking an important transition from principles to implementation.

Building on the Secretary-General’s Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals—which received strong support from Member States—we are now focused on turning its Guiding Principles and Recommendations into action.

One message came through loud and clear:

The clean energy transition must not repeat the mistakes of the past.

Countries endowed with critical mineral resources want more than extraction. They want to create value at home through processing, manufacturing, industrialization, skills development, quality jobs and sustainable investment. They want their mineral wealth to become a foundation for long-term prosperity.

Another message was equally powerful.

No government can achieve this alone.

Building resilient, responsible and equitable mineral value chains requires governments, industry, investors, Indigenous Peoples, workers, local communities, civil society, development finance institutions and international organizations working together.

This is where the United Nations has a unique role to play.

Through the UN Task Force and its Country Support Mechanism, more than 20 UN entities and international organizations are joining forces to help countries strengthen governance, mobilize investment, develop value-addition strategies, build institutional capacity and ensure that critical energy transition minerals become a driver of sustainable development.

At a time of growing geopolitical competition, this agenda demonstrates that international cooperation remains indispensable.

The race for critical minerals must not become a race to the bottom. It must become a race to create more value, more opportunity and more shared prosperity.

That is the vision that brought governments together this week. Now comes the harder—and more important—task: delivering results on the ground.

My sincere thanks to all Member States and to our colleagues across UNDP, UN Environment Programme , UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) , United Nations Development Coordination Office (UNDCO), UNIDO,  the UN Regional Commissions, and The World Bank Group  for their leadership and collaboration as we move from vision to implementation.

subsidies, 
weak cost recovery, 
underfunded utilities 
grids struggling to maintain themselves.

diesel exposure, 
fuel imports, 
small grid scale, 
island economics
limited generation diversity.

Downtime cover.

What is the C&I price?
How reliable is the grid?
How much subsidy is hidden?
How much backup power is still required?
How does purchasing power change the ranking?

For African power users, the real energy question goes beyond price.

Can AI become a catalyst for sustainable development without becoming a growing burden on the planet?

That was the central question from today’s 2026 HLPF side event on Advancing Digital Environmental Sustainability for SDG Implementation. As the HLPF draws to a close, the discussion reinforced that digital transformation must be integrated into the sustainable development agenda.

AI is reshaping development, but behind every algorithm lies a physical system powered by electricity, water, minerals and infrastructure. By 2030, data centres could use 945 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent of the current electricity consumption of Africa.

By 2030, AI is expected to add US$15.7 trillion to the global economy, while developing countries may capture only 10% of that value.

I shared insights from UNDP ’s report, The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries, which shows that AI’s next frontier will depend as much on energy systems as computing power. It calls for Green AI that advances people, protects the planet and expands prosperity by aligning digital investment with clean energy and national priorities.

I shared three key priorities: directing AI towards practical development challenges, building skills and innovation ecosystems that create domestic value, and embedding sustainability and accountability into investment from the outset.

Examples are emerging. In Kenya, AI-enabled energy systems are improving affordability and resilience. In Moldova, UNDP is supporting 500,000 smart meters by 2030. UNDP tools, such as the Clean Energy Equity Index and the Electricity Access Forecasting Model, are helping countries improve AI and digital planning and resilience.

My takeaway is that the Global Digital Compact must move from ambition to implementation. Beyond 2030, digital progress should be defined not by technological scale alone, but by its contribution to inclusion, resilience and sustainable development. #UNDP #HLPF2026 #GreenAI #DigitalSustainability

HLPF 2026: SDG7 had its stocktake. Now the final four years have to prove what access actually enables.

One week on from the HLPF review of #SDG7 , the outcome gave energy the political weight it deserves. It treated SDG7 not just as an energy target, but as a test of whether sustainable development can still deliver by 2030. The remaining gap will not be closed by ambition alone; it’ll be closed through the practical choices now made on access, clean cooking, grids, storage, finance, partnerships and women’s leadership.

But the data cut through that language…

…Because the reality is that global electricity access has stalled at 92%, while ~1.18 billion people remain energy poor, including ~447 million who are officially connected but still unable to use electricity meaningfully... That is the SDG7 blind spot for the final four years: access on paper is not the same as affordable, reliable power that supports productive use, resilience and dignity.📣‼️

Time will tell whether this stocktake becomes a turning point for delivery; not just stronger language, but a different test of what access enables, who benefits and who remains outside the system:

1️⃣ Access has to be judged by what it enables. A connection is not the finish line. SDG7 has to mean affordability, reliability, clean cooking, productive use, resilience, livelihoods and dignity.

2️⃣ Delivery has to connect the systems around energy. Finance, grids, skills, industrial strategy, digital demand and labour markets cannot keep moving as separate conversations. That is where implementation either scales or fails.

3️⃣ Data has to expose the gaps that averages hide. If this transition is meant to be just, gender-responsive and intergenerationally inclusive, then we need to know who benefits, who leads, who carries the burden and who remains invisible.

That is the real test after this stocktake: whether SDG7 can move from progress language into delivery systems that reach the people and places still outside them. #EnergyKiltMan #HLPF2026 #SDG7 #JustTransition #EnergyAccess

What does mineral security mean if mineral-rich countries remain at the lowest-value end of the supply chain?

Following last week's first UN High-Level Meeting on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, attention is rightly focused on building more resilient and diversified supply chains.

But I have increasingly come to see mineral security as more than securing supply. It must also be about where value is created, who develops the technology and skills, and whether communities share in the benefits of the transition. This is particularly important for many countries across the Global South that supply critical minerals for renewable energy, battery storage and e-mobility.

Critical minerals have moved from being solely an energy issue to becoming an energy, economic and national security issue. As demand for clean energy technologies continues to grow, the opportunity for producing countries extends far beyond mining. If Latin America refined its lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths domestically—and processed two-thirds of its copper—the economic value generated could increase by nearly 50%, reaching approximately USD 220 billion by 2035.

This points to a broader shift: from exporting raw materials to building regional value chains, developing manufacturing capacity, creating skilled jobs and strengthening economic resilience. It also requires investment, technology, workforce development, international cooperation and traceability to build transparent, trusted and resilient value chains that attract investment while ensuring producing countries capture a greater share of the benefits.

South-South cooperation can help make this transformation possible by connecting mineral resources with shared infrastructure, knowledge, investment and markets.

Critical minerals must power development, not reproduce dependency.

The measure of mineral security is not only supply. It is shared prosperity.

In 1949, the world was home to 2.2 billion people. Today, we are more than 8.2 billion. Every week, the world's population grows by roughly 1.3 million people—equivalent to adding a city the size of Prague every seven days. Almost all of that growth is taking place in developing economies. By 2050, these countries are expected to account for around 85% of global energy demand growth. 

The future of the energy transition will therefore be shaped where populations, cities and industries are expanding the fastest.
These demographic trends are reshaping the geography of development, investment and opportunity.

I was pleased to contribute to the discussion during the #HLPF last week "From Vulnerability to Investment: Overcoming Barriers to Energy Access, Resilient Infrastructure and Green Industrialization in LDCs," co-organized by Nepal, the State of Qatar, UN-OHRLLS and UNIDO.

A just energy transition should not be seen only as a pathway to decarbonization, but as a vehicle to strengthen energy security, build economic resilience, and preserve the natural systems on which future development depends.

Countries such as Bhutan and Nepal demonstrate what is possible. In Bhutan, hydropower has become a pillar of economic development and exports. In Nepal, more than 400 community micro-hydro systems have provided electricity to over 500,000 people while supporting more than 1,000 rural enterprises. Energy has created businesses, incomes and opportunities—not just electricity connections.Those examples show the importance of creating the right conditions for investment. 

Expanding domestic renewable energy can reduce exposure to volatile fuel imports—where a 50% increase in oil prices could add around US$16 billion to LDC import bills. Regional power markets can unlock larger investment opportunities, while better de-risking and blended finance can mobilize private capital where financing costs remain the main barrier. 

In The Gambia, a UNDP-supported mini-grid commissioned this year supplies electricity to 375 households and more than 75 small businesses—from welders and tailors to cold storage—demonstrating how energy access can become an investable local economy. In Zambia, the national electrification agency is co-financing a new electrification programme with an investment nearly ten times larger than the UNDP-managed grant, illustrating how catalytic finance can mobilize domestic resources and scale impact.

The impact of a just energy transition should ultimately be measured not only by the number of people connected, but by the jobs it creates, the resilience it builds, the nature it preserves, and the economic opportunities it unlocks. US$2 trillion was invested in clean energy globally last year, yet international public clean energy finance for developing countries amounted to just US$24.6 billion.
 
At today's Building Investment Plans to Unlock Climate Finance for Vulnerable Nations dialogue at #HLPF2026 , I posed a simple question: Are SIDS and LDCs truly lacking bankable projects, or are we failing to recognize where value is being created?
 
The economics of the energy transition are increasingly compelling. Renewable electricity costs are projected to fall 30% by 2030, while electricity demand over the next five years is expected to grow 50% faster than over the previous decade. Capital is available. Demand is growing.
 
The opportunity is to connect the two.
 
That starts with better data. UNDP's satellite analysis identified 1.18 billion people living in energy poverty, around 60% more than those captured by conventional electricity access metrics. Better intelligence helps reveal hidden demand, reduce investment risk, and direct finance where it can deliver the greatest development impact.
 
It also means financing economic value creation. Clean energy should power industries, transport, agriculture, and digital economies that create jobs and strengthen resilience. This matters because manufacturing value added per capita in LDCs has increased by more than 40% since 2015, yet it remains far below the global average.
 
It also requires the right conditions for private investment. With around 80% of public clean energy finance coming as debt and only 5% supporting risk mitigation, countries need policy reform, blended finance, and tools like UNDP’s Energy Finance Innovation Labs to build investable pipelines and reduce risk.
 
Investment plans become bankable pipelines when we stop financing energy as a standalone asset and start financing the economic value it unlocks.
 
That is UNDP 's role: helping countries build the institutions, markets, and investment ecosystems that turn clean energy into jobs, industries, resilience, and long-term development.
 
My thanks to SEforALL and the Governments of Australia, Barbados, Fiji, and Tuvalu for convening this timely dialogue ahead of Pre-COP31 and for advancing the broader conversation on unlocking climate finance for vulnerable countries in the lead-up to COP31. #EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #PreCOP31 #RisingUpForSIDS

What does it mean for the energy transition to reach the grid, the data centre and the electric vehicle, but still not reach the kitchen?
 
Today’s discussion brought that challenge into focus at the 2026 HLPF Regional Satellite Event, “From Commitment to Implementation: A Regional Dialogue on Coordinated UN-Energy Action for Clean Cooking.”
 
Clean cooking remains one of the most urgent and overlooked development challenges. While the world is investing over US$2.2 trillion in the energy transition, 2 billion people still cook with polluting fuels, and 1.8 billion are projected to remain without clean cooking in 2030.
 
The discussions made clear that clean cooking sits at the heart of health, gender equality, climate action and human dignity. Household air pollution caused 2.9 million deaths in 2021, including 309,000 children under five, while women and girls continue to carry the burden of smoke exposure and fuel collection.
 
Yet progress is possible: since 2010, India, China and Indonesia have driven 80% of the global reduction in the clean cooking access gap.
 
The conversation also reinforced the need for smarter, more targeted delivery. Of the 2 billion people without clean cooking access, 1.5 billion live in rural areas, and the top 20 access-deficit countries account for around three-quarters of the global gap. Using geospatial analytics and AI-driven tools such as the Clean Energy Equity Index, UNDP helps countries identify underserved communities and target clean energy investments where they are needed most.
 
But delivery also needs finance and systems that can turn commitments into results. Universal clean cooking access requires around US$8 billion annually, while the cost of inaction is estimated at US$2.4 trillion each year. Examples from Ghana, Rwanda and Morocco show how clear targets, public finance and delivery systems can move clean cooking from pledge to practice.
 
I left the discussion with one clear reflection: the energy transition cannot be judged only by how much power we generate, but by whether it reaches the kitchens, classrooms, clinics and communities still being left behind. #HLPF2026 #SDG7 #CleanCooking #CleanEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #UNEnergy #UNDP

⚡ Renewables can do more than generate clean power. Combined with modern grids, storage and digital intelligence, they can deliver reliable energy for people.
 
In 2025, the world added a record 692 GW of renewable power capacity, alongside 108 GW of new battery storage, 40% more than the year before.  
 
Together, these investments create a major opportunity. Grids can move electricity where it is needed, storage can make it available beyond the hours when the sun shines or the wind blows, and digital tools can help systems respond to changing supply and demand.
 
For people, that means health facilities that keep operating, schools that stay connected, businesses that can grow and communities that are better prepared for disruption.
 
Uruguay shows what coordinated investment can achieve. Through long-term policy, public investment and power-system planning, the country reached a 98% share of renewables in its electricity mix in 2019.
 
For me, this is how energy progress should be measured: not only by how much clean power a system can produce, but by how reliably it improves people’s lives.
 
For close to 1 billion people served by health facilities with unreliable electricity or none at all, reliability determines whether vaccines stay cold, medical equipment works and essential care continues.  
 
Three investments can unlock this opportunity:
 
🌍 Modern and decentralized grids bring clean energy closer to people, connecting generation, storage and demand while helping essential services withstand disruptions.
 
🔋 Storage makes variable power dependable, capturing electricity when supply is abundant and releasing it when demand rises.
 
📊 Digital management adds flexibility. Better forecasting and digitally enabled demand response could reduce renewable curtailment by more than 25% by 2030.

What does my mother's couscous teaches us about industrial policy? 

Well, a lot, as it turns out! My mother, Fatima, is like the East Asian 'miracle'. You can try to copy her recipes, but you will probably will not get the same results. It turns out that what make her cuisine brilliant is that she can easily adapt and change it based on the ingredients and ustentils she has access to. She has never shared a recipe without explaining "if you have X, do Y. If not, do Z". And for industrial policy, it is the same: success is not defined by the quality of policy instrument or budgets, as much as the capacity of the cook to adapt and change the recipe based on changing conditions and institutional constraints. What is also means is that industrial policy is a living dynamic system that needs to constantly learning and adjust, not a blueprint. 

I am glad this piece (drawn from recent research for UNU-WIDER - United Nations University World Institute for Development Economics Research is part of the 50-year anniversary book of the The OPEC Fund for International Development . In 2019, Ghana launched the Year of Return, a nationwide campaign commemorating 400 years since the first enslaved Africans were taken from its shores. Backed by a $3.5 million investment, the initiative encouraged Africans in the diaspora to reconnect with their heritage through festivals, cultural events, and visits to historic sites such as Cape Coast Castle. The campaign attracted global figures including Idris Elba, Naomi Campbell , and Steve Harvey , while visitor arrivals surged 45%, average tourist spending increased from $1,862 to $2,589, and tourism generated an estimated $1.9 billion for the Ghanaian economy.

Rather than ending after one year, Ghana expanded the initiative into Beyond the Return, a 10-year program running through 2030 aimed at strengthening long-term ties with the African diaspora. The country also reinforced its commitment through policies allowing people of African descent in the Americas to reside indefinitely in Ghana. Since then, citizenship ceremonies have accelerated, with around 1,500 people choosing to permanently relocate, while diaspora buyers now account for nearly 30% of high-end property purchases in Accra.

Ghana's approach demonstrates how cultural heritage can be transformed into a long-term economic strategy. By using tourism as an entry point to encourage citizenship, real estate investment, and entrepreneurship, the country has positioned itself as a leading destination for the African diaspora seeking to reconnect with the continent. The success of the initiative has also inspired broader conversations across Africa about attracting diaspora talent, investment, and expertise to support the continent's development.

“We’re not in an energy transition. We’re in an energy addition.” It’s a good line. And it has some serious people behind it who point out that fossil fuels still supply around 80% of global energy, barely down from 85% in 1990, while fossil demand keeps growing.

They have a point. Historically, clean energy has scaled too slowly to replace more fossil demand than the world adds each year. In absolute global primary energy terms, it looks like renewables have just been added on top.

But the argument draws the wrong conclusion, for two reasons.

First, global aggregates hide almost everything that matters. Look sectorally and regionally and you see systems already changing beyond recognition — EVs in Norway, batteries in California, solar in Pakistan, gas phasing down in Spain, heat pumps across the Nordics. Since 2016, clean energy has attracted more investment every year than fossil fuels, now roughly double. Around 90% of new power capacity is renewable. Nearly one in five cars sold worldwide is fully electric.

Second, and more fundamentally, the “80%” is based on a measurement error. It counts primary energy — but around two thirds of that is lost as waste heat in combustion before it delivers any useful service. Measuring the system this way inflates fossil fuels and understates both the efficiency of renewables and the demand we avoid through electrification. The share of useful energy (energy services) that clean energy provides is much larger than its share of primary energy consumption.

As World Water Week 2026 continues in Stockholm under the theme "Water for People and Progress," this is the question I keep coming back to: AI is no longer only an energy story.
 
By 2027, AI is projected to withdraw 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water annually, up to six times Denmark's total annual water withdrawal. Cooling is a major part of the equation. Data centres generate enormous amounts of heat, and removing that heat can require significant volumes of water, especially in hot climates.
 
I have come to see this as a siting and governance question rather than a technology one. Where digital infrastructure is built, and under what rules, will determine whether it strengthens or strains local water systems.
Three approaches are worth watching:
 
📐 Set measurable standards. Singapore's Green Data Center Roadmap prioritises energy efficiency and cooling technologies suited to tropical climates, and steers new development toward areas with cleaner grids and more abundant resources.
 
💧 Make water conditions part of approval. Malaysia, South-East Asia's most water-stressed country, has more than 100 proposed data centres that could consume over 808 million litres a day. Regulators now require all new facilities to use only recycled, reclaimed or rainwater as a condition of approval.
 
🌍 Plan for local conditions, not imported models. In Asia and the Pacific, water-use effectiveness averages 1.65 litres per kilowatt-hour, more than three times the global average of 0.5. Cooling strategies that work in Stockholm will not work in Kuala Lumpur.
 
For countries across the Global South, the opportunity is not simply to host the next generation of digital infrastructure, but to shape how it is powered, cooled and governed.
 
The AI revolution will be judged not only by what it computes, but by what it consumes.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #WorldWaterWeek

⚡ What if the path to universal energy access is not about choosing between grid and off-grid solutions, but planning them together?
 
That question is becoming more urgent. Electricity demand from data centres is set to more than double by 2030, reaching around 945 TWh. In several emerging data-centre hubs, AI infrastructure already accounts for 5 to 20 percent of total electricity demand.
For developing countries, digital growth can crowd in investment and modernise power systems, or compete with households, clinics and small businesses for limited electricity. The outcome depends on how power systems are planned today.
 
New analysis across Burkina Faso, Mali, Nigeria and Senegal shows why this matters. Where grid expansion is constrained, mini-grids can serve between 47 million and 110 million people out of 171 million needing access, accounting for more than half of new connections in some scenarios.
 
Battery storage can strengthen that pathway. Across the scenarios assessed, fuel savings average around US$2 for every US$1 of additional storage investment. Under optimistic mini-grid costs at Tier 2–3 demand levels, savings can reach up to US$4 for every US$1 invested by reducing diesel generation.
 
For me, the lesson is that grid extension, mini-grids, storage and digital infrastructure cannot be planned in isolation. Digital demand is reshaping power-system needs, while grids and storage determine how that growth can be served.
 
For countries still closing their access gaps, the opportunity is to plan grids, storage and digital growth together, so that rising demand expands access and opportunity rather than competing for scarce power.
 
🔗 Further reading: IRENA, Unlocking battery storage potential for sustainable mini-grid electrification in West Africa
https://bit.ly/4ynideG
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyAccess

⚡ What does development look like in an age when electricity is becoming more important to the global economy, but 655 million people still live without it?
 
As the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opens today, the world is entering what the IEA calls the “Age of Electricity.”
 
🌍 92% of the world now has access to electricity. Yet 655 million people remain without it — and 86% of them live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
🍳 2 billion people still rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, including 970 million in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
⚡ Meanwhile, global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6% annually through 2030, adding around 1,100 TWh each year.
 
💻 Data centres alone could consume around 945 TWh by 2030, more than double today’s level.
 
☀️ Renewables now provide over 30% of global electricity. But renewable generating capacity averages just 33.6 watts per person in low-income countries, compared with 1,224 watts in high-income countries — a gap of more than 36 times.
 
For me, these numbers point to a fundamental development challenge: we are building an increasingly electrified global economy, but we are not yet building it equally.
 
AI, data centres, advanced manufacturing, electric mobility and cooling are increasing the value of reliable power. Yet where energy could unlock some of the greatest development gains, hundreds of millions still lack basic access.
 
The energy transition therefore cannot be measured only in gigawatts installed or emissions avoided. We also need to ask where new capacity is built, who can access it, and what opportunities it creates.
 
As leaders gather in New York, the opportunity is to make this “Age of Electricity” an age of development too — expanding access, creating jobs and investment, and enabling more countries to participate in the industries shaping the global economy.
 
The real measure of the energy transition will not only be how much energy we produce, but how widely its opportunities are shared.
 
#UNGA81 #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #SDG7

⚡The energy transition is about Jobs. But where and for who ?
 
Renewable energy employment reached a record 16.6 million jobs globally in 2024.
 
Yet more than 85% of those jobs are concentrated in just five countries and regions.
 
That raises a bigger question: the energy transition is creating enormous economic value — but who will have the opportunity to create, own and benefit from it?
 
A just transition is not only about creating more green jobs.
 
🏭 It is about socio-economic development, where new industries and supply chains are built. Between 2018 and 2024, China accounted for around 80% of global investment in manufacturing facilities for solar, wind, batteries and hydrogen technologies.
 
💰 It is about where investment flows. Low- and lower-middle-income countries are home to more than 40% of the world’s population, yet account for only 7% of global clean energy spending. In emerging and developing economies, the cost of capital for renewable energy projects can be two to three times higher than in advanced economies.
 
👷 It is about whether workers can access the opportunities being created. Around 60% of energy companies report labour shortages, and the number of graduates entering the energy sector would need to increase by around 40% by 2030 just to prevent today’s skills mismatch from worsening.
 
⚡ And it is about whether the transition ultimately delivers for people and planet. Even as clean energy investment and employment reach record levels, 655 million people worldwide still live without electricity.
 
These numbers are connected.
 
Where investment and manufacturing concentrate, jobs and economic value tend to follow.
 
For developing economies, a just transition must therefore be about more than replacing one energy source with another. It must help create decent jobs, build local industries and skills, expand affordable and reliable energy access, mobilize investment and support economic diversification.
 
As #UNGA81 gathers momentum, the question is not only how fast we can move. It is how we ensure more countries, communities and people can participate in creating the value generated by the transition — and share in its benefits.
 
Speed matters. But so does where the transition takes us — and who gets there with us.
 
#JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

⚡ What does development look like in an age when electricity is becoming more important to the global economy, but 655 million people still live without it?
 
As the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opens today, the world is entering what the IEA calls the “Age of Electricity.”
 
🌍 92% of the world now has access to electricity. Yet 655 million people remain without it — and 86% of them live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
🍳 2 billion people still rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, including 970 million in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
⚡ Meanwhile, global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6% annually through 2030, adding around 1,100 TWh each year.
 
💻 Data centres alone could consume around 945 TWh by 2030, more than double today’s level.
 
☀️ Renewables now provide over 30% of global electricity. But renewable generating capacity averages just 33.6 watts per person in low-income countries, compared with 1,224 watts in high-income countries — a gap of more than 36 times.
 
For me, these numbers point to a fundamental development challenge: we are building an increasingly electrified global economy, but we are not yet building it equally.
 
AI, data centres, advanced manufacturing, electric mobility and cooling are increasing the value of reliable power. Yet where energy could unlock some of the greatest development gains, hundreds of millions still lack basic access.
 
The energy transition therefore cannot be measured only in gigawatts installed or emissions avoided. We also need to ask where new capacity is built, who can access it, and what opportunities it creates.
 
As leaders gather in New York, the opportunity is to make this “Age of Electricity” an age of development too — expanding access, creating jobs and investment, and enabling more countries to participate in the industries shaping the global economy.
 
The real measure of the energy transition will not only be how much energy we produce, but how widely its opportunities are shared. #UNGA81 #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #SDG7

Could clean cooking be one of the most powerful opportunities to advance health, gender equality and sustainable development?
 
On the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies, I keep coming back to clean cooking.
 
Nearly 2 billion people still lack access to clean cooking. In rural Sub-Saharan Africa, only 7% of the population has access to clean cooking fuels.
 
The consequences reach far beyond the kitchen. Household air pollution caused an estimated 2.9 million deaths in 2021, while polluting cooking also affects productivity, gender equality and economic opportunity.
 
Yet the investment gap remains striking.
 
Around US$2.5 billion is invested in clean cooking solutions each year, less than a third of the US$8 billion needed annually to achieve universal access. Meanwhile, the health, environmental and productivity costs associated with polluting cooking are estimated at US$2.4–4 trillion every year.
 
For me, this makes clean cooking not simply an energy technology, but a development priority across the Global South.
 
Three shifts can help accelerate progress:
🔌 Integrate clean cooking into national energy planning. Nepal aims for 25% of households to adopt electric cooking by 2030, linking clean cooking directly to wider electrification efforts.
💰 Make finance reach the households most often left behind. Grants, subsidies and blended finance can help reduce upfront costs for rural and low-income communities.
🗺️ Use data and digital tools to target solutions better. Mapping grid reliability, consumer demand and e-cooking potential can help direct investment where it can deliver the greatest impact.
 
Clean air, energy access and development should not be treated as separate agendas.
 
Clean cooking can improve health, expand opportunity and make a just energy transition more inclusive at the same time.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #CleanCooking #CleanAir

⚡The energy transition is about Jobs. But where and for who ?
 
Renewable energy employment reached a record 16.6 million jobs globally in 2024.
 
Yet more than 85% of those jobs are concentrated in just five countries and regions.
 
That raises a bigger question: the energy transition is creating enormous economic value — but who will have the opportunity to create, own and benefit from it?
 
A just transition is not only about creating more green jobs.
 
🏭 It is about socio-economic development, where new industries and supply chains are built. Between 2018 and 2024, China accounted for around 80% of global investment in manufacturing facilities for solar, wind, batteries and hydrogen technologies.
 
💰 It is about where investment flows. Low- and lower-middle-income countries are home to more than 40% of the world’s population, yet account for only 7% of global clean energy spending. In emerging and developing economies, the cost of capital for renewable energy projects can be two to three times higher than in advanced economies.
 
👷 It is about whether workers can access the opportunities being created. Around 60% of energy companies report labour shortages, and the number of graduates entering the energy sector would need to increase by around 40% by 2030 just to prevent today’s skills mismatch from worsening.
 
⚡ And it is about whether the transition ultimately delivers for people and planet. Even as clean energy investment and employment reach record levels, 655 million people worldwide still live without electricity.
 
These numbers are connected.
 
Where investment and manufacturing concentrate, jobs and economic value tend to follow.
 
For developing economies, a just transition must therefore be about more than replacing one energy source with another. It must help create decent jobs, build local industries and skills, expand affordable and reliable energy access, mobilize investment and support economic diversification.
 
As #UNGA81 gathers momentum, the question is not only how fast we can move. It is how we ensure more countries, communities and people can participate in creating the value generated by the transition — and share in its benefits.
 
Speed matters. But so does where the transition takes us — and who gets there with us. #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

What if the strongest case for greening our operations is what clean energy enables beyond carbon?

UNDP’s new Greening Moonshot report offers a useful answer.

Halfway to 2030, we have reduced operational emissions by 25 percent compared with 2018. More than 200 projects now reduce over 4,000 tonnes of CO₂e each year while saving nearly $2 million annually in energy costs. Every $1 invested in green energy solutions now delivers around $8.5 in lifetime energy savings.

But the development story goes further.

⚡ Reliable energy enables delivery. In Afghanistan, more than 370 kWp of solar capacity is reducing dependence on diesel where the national grid is unreliable. In Haiti, renewable energy supplies around two-thirds of office power through chronic blackouts and fuel shortages.

💰 Efficiency creates development resources. Greening investments have enabled more than $21 million to be reprogrammed to country priorities.

📊 Data makes the transition smarter. Different energy systems require different solutions. Solar and batteries make sense for generator-dependent offices. E-mobility can deliver greater gains where electricity is already clean.

This is why I increasingly see clean energy as development infrastructure.

It keeps teams working, reduces exposure to energy shocks and frees resources for the communities we serve.

The energy transition succeeds when it improves how development is delivered.

#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanEnergy #ClimateAction #GreeningMoonshot

AI is creating a global race for power. Governments are moving quickly to build generation, grids and dedicated capacity for data centres. That urgency should extend to the energy needed by schools, hospitals, farms and businesses.

On 23 September, I will join the IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit during New York Climate Week to discuss The Role of AI in Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition.

The numbers show how quickly the energy landscape is changing:

Data-centre electricity consumption could almost double between 2025 and 2030, rising from around 485 TWh to 950 TWh.

More than 100 GW of new gas capacity is planned as dedicated onsite supply for data centres. Almost all of it is in the United States, with around 13 GW announced or under development elsewhere.

Middle-income countries generate around half of ChatGPT traffic, while low- and middle-income countries host only about one-quarter of global data-centre capacity.

AI is a double-edged sword for energy systems. It can improve renewable forecasting, grid management, efficiency and investment planning. It can also drive major new electricity demand, make fossil-fuel extraction cheaper and more productive, and extend dependence on existing fuels. Policies, safeguards and financing decisions will determine which effects dominate.

I look forward to discussing how countries can shape this expansion around their own development priorities: building additional clean power, strengthening grids, protecting people and ecosystems, and ensuring that the infrastructure and value created are more widely shared.

#ClimateWeekNYC #ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableAI
